https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjaexcf.text: An Israeli man in his 30s was stabbed early Tuesday at the Ozora music festival in Hungary, while two other Israelis were arrested in a separate incident on suspicion of attempting to sell drugs to an undercover police officer. Hungarian police arrested three suspects in connection with the stabbing. Authorities said the Israeli victim was hospitalized and that his condition had stabilized. Following the attack, police said they had increased their presence at the festival grounds and would continue carrying out heightened security checks with the event’s organizers to protect attendees. The three suspects are being investigated over their alleged involvement in a serious assault and on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm. It was not the first stabbing involving an Israeli at the festival. Last year, a 26-year-old Israeli was wounded on the final day of the event after allegedly being attacked by another Israeli. In a separate case, Hungarian authorities said police arrested three people at the festival on Monday, including two Israelis, after allegedly catching them selling drugs. One of the Israelis is a survivor of the Nova music festival massacre on October 7 and is believed to suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder. Attorney Mordechai Tzivin, who specializes in assisting Israelis arrested abroad, said he expected the detainees’ rights to be protected. “Based on my experience in Hungary, the young men are fortunate that the incident did not occur under the previous government,” he said. “It can be assumed that under the current political circumstances, law enforcement authorities will act in the accepted, independent and fair manner seen in European Union countries, free from pressure. This will presumably also be reflected in the protection of detainees’ rights.”

https://speedcafe.com/f1-news-2026-itali.text: Login Register HOME NEWS PODS PHOTOS RESULTS NETWORK 100 SUPERCARS F1 MOTOGP NASCAR INDYCAR GT & ENDURANCE KARTING RALLY DRAGS SPEEDWAY HOME NEWS PODS PHOTOS RESULTS NETWORK 100 Feed Calendar Results Photos Podcasts Shop Supercars F1 NASCAR IndyCar GT & Endurance Karting Bikes Rally Drags Speedway McLaren confirms rotating ‘H-Wing’ for Italian GP McLaren will race its own rotating rear wing for the first time at this weekend’s Italian Grand Prix as it continues the aggressive development of its MCL40. Dubbed the ‘H-Wing’, the device will form part of a low-drag package designed specifically for Monza’s long straights and high-speed layout. McLaren first tested the concept during opening practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix in July, having previously taken an earlier version to Austria without running it on track . The system allows the rear wing to rotate between its cornering and straight-line configurations, reducing drag when the car is travelling at high speed. Ferrari first introduced its own interpretation of the concept during pre-season testing before Red Bull followed with a version at Miami . McLaren will now put its design into competitive use at Monza, with both cars set to have the H-Wing available from Friday practice. The unusual name is a deliberate reference to one of the team’s best-known technical innovations. McLaren’s 2010 F-duct took its name from the ‘F’ in Vodafone branding positioned near the system’s inlet, with the team applying the same thinking to its latest development. “The H-Wing’s naming convention pays homage to McLaren’s innovative F-duct, which debuted in 2010 and took its name from the ‘F’ in the branding positioned alongside the system’s inlet on the car,” McLaren explained. “In the same spirit, the H-Wing is named after the ‘H’ in Etihad Airways branding displayed on the rear wing as part of the team’s partnership with the airline.” A post shared by McLaren Mastercard Formula 1 Team 🧡 (@mclarenf1) The H-Wing will not be McLaren’s only new option in Italy, with the team also bringing a fresh low-drag rear wing specification and several smaller aerodynamic changes. Technical director of applied engineering Neil Houldey said the components would be assessed through practice before McLaren settles on its qualifying configuration. “This weekend, we have brought what we believe is needed to be competitive, including a new low-drag rear wing specification, including the first use of our H-Wing, alongside some small aerodynamic and low-drag options that we will evaluate before deciding the final specification for qualifying,” Houldey said. “Overall, we know there is still more performance to unlock from the MCL40, both through maximising the package we already have and through further upgrades planned for the races ahead.” The changes continue a sustained development push which has coincided with McLaren’s strongest run of the 2026 season. A major package introduced in Hungary included a new floor and several accompanying aerodynamic revisions, helping Lando Norris claim the team’s first victory of the year . McLaren then added a new rear wing and revised rear brake ducts at Zandvoort, where Norris backed up his Hungary success with a second consecutive win . Houldey said Monza’s unique characteristics would provide a different test for the team. “Monza presents a unique challenge, with its long straights placing a premium on drag reduction, while the heavy braking zones demand stability and the chicanes require good ride performance,” he said. “Energy will also be limited around the lap, so understanding the best way to recharge and deploy it will be an important focus during practice.” McLaren will also run a slightly revised livery at Monza as part of its ongoing partnership with cryptocurrency exchange OKX, with the enhancement set to return at next week’s Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid. FP1 for the Italian Grand Prix gets underway at 8.30pm AEST Friday. Europe Home page Europe 0 0 Slovakian troops not going to fight Russia for those seeking conflict — premier 20 September 2026 06:40 (UTC +04:00) The government of Slovakia will not send its soldiers to fight against Russia based on a fabricated pretext and on behalf of those who are fueling the conflict with Moscow, Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico said, APA reports. "If someone is interested in provoking a military conflict between NATO and Russia to satisfy their own national interests, they must bear the responsibility for such a move, instead of shifting it onto other NATO members," the premier said in a video address posted on Facebook. "It’s easy to create a pretext to begin a war. However, we are mature enough to distinguish an armed attack by a non-NATO country on one or more NATO member states from something entirely different," the premier continued. "As long as my government remains in office, no one will send Slovak soldiers outside of Slovakia to fight against Russia or any other country based on a fabricated pretext." Besides, Fico urged "to stop the rhetoric of false solidarity" among members of the European Union. He added that anti-Russian calls in the West are aimed at distracting attention from domestic problems. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the ‘deep anxiety’ of young people in his address to the nation but he has few fiscal options. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the ‘deep anxiety’ of young people in his address to the nation but he has few fiscal options. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/AFP/Getty Images France Analysis Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation Jon Henley in Paris French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profound Europe live – latest updates Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.33 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.55 EDT Share The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is. Speaking from his office at the Élysée Palace, the president delivered an eight-minute speech expressing “anger and shame” after a weekend in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured. A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement . French prime minister calls for ‘local and partial’ curfews after riots Read more Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille. Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand. The response, across the political spectrum, was damning. The Greens’ leader, Marine Tondelier, said that rather than “even beginning to make any kind of mea culpa”, Macron was “summoning us to the PM’s office like pupils to the blackboard”. On the far right, the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella called the speech “lamentable” and said Macron had “nothing left to say” to the French. The party’s figurehead, Marine Le Pen, said the country was “caught in a vice between violence and impotence”. The centre-right’s Bruno Retailleau said Macron was “totally overwhelmed”, while on the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the president of relying on “inaction and police brutality” in doomed hopes that the protests would simply fizzle out. Perhaps most damagingly, even Macron’s former prime minister Édouard Philippe said he would have preferred “decisions and initiatives that might lead to a return to order and the restoration of state authority … Our country needs to be governed.” Criticism is to be expected from rivals positioning themselves six months before a presidential election to choose Macron’s successor. But its sheer ferocity underlines his isolation, the disdain in which he is held, and the anger he inspires. It is a structural trap that he has largely set for himself. Macron came to power in 2017 as a “Jupiterian” president – a deliberate strategy aimed at elevating the head of state above daily politics, projecting distant authority and technocratic brilliance. But over nine years in the Élysée, that high-handed style – partly born, his critics say, of Macron’s complete lack of basic political experience as an elected official in a town hall or as a constituency MP – has morphed into perceived arrogance and detachment. It has been compounded by catastrophic strategic errors, and France’s spiralling economic problems. Macron lost a functional parliamentary majority by refusing to meaningfully campaign between the presidential and legislative elections of 2022. Two years later he dissolved the national assembly. That gamble backfired spectacularly, with voters returning an even more deadlocked parliament split between a divided left, a much-diminished centrist bloc and Le Pen’s far right. Without a working majority, the government repeatedly resorted to controversial constitutional manoeuvres to force through laws without a parliamentary vote, laying it – and Macron – open to further accusations of democratic illegitimacy. Compounding that institutional deadlock is a looming fiscal crisis. In decades gone by, French presidents facing mass protests on the streets could in effect buy a degree of social tranquility with targeted spending packages or public sector concessions. But France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946 . Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday. French debt chart The markets are worried : France’s borrowing costs are higher than Greece’s. And with few fiscal options, the government’s clearest response – in time-honoured French tradition – has been teargas and baton charges, sometimes against schoolchildren, further aggravating tensions. The consequences for the presidential election could be profound. The centrist coalition built around Macron’s brand has all but collapsed. If the protests and violence persist, the main beneficiary will be the law-and-order champions of the far right. Jean-Baptiste Moreau, an influential former MP from Macron’s party with whom the largely lame-duck president still occasionally speaks, reportedly went so far this weekend as to suggest he should resign and call early presidential elections. “Macron still thinks he can change things,” he told Le Monde . “But at the moment, Marine Le Pen is on a direct path to the Élysée Palace.” Explore more on these topics France Emmanuel Macron Europe Protest analysis Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story In his final UN speech, Macron may have given other leaders a valuable parting gift: the guts to stand up to Trump ‘Very naive’: French left up in arms as Macron hosts Trump at Versailles ‘You have to be serious’: Macron criticises Trump’s mixed messages about Nato and Iran ‘Not up to standard’: Macron criticises Trump after comments about his marriage ‘Not a typical day’: makers of Macron’s sunglasses deluged with demand Ten people go on trial in Paris accused of online harassment of Brigitte Macron Macrons to submit scientific evidence to US court to prove Brigitte was not born a man Emmanuel Macron appoints his third prime minister in a year Bayrou’s fall and a divided parliament hardly offer the stability Macron needs Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

He says Aisle has been more effective at defending critical infrastructure 'than many of the more well known efforts.' Fred Lum/The Globe and Mail Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create an account Cohere Inc. is acquiring European startup Aisle to bolster its cybersecurity capabilities as the artificial-intelligence industry grapples with the technology’s potential to both defend against threats and conduct more sophisticated hacks if used by bad actors. Toronto-based Cohere said on Thursday that it had signed a letter of intent to acquire Aisle, which is based in Prague. Financial terms were not disclosed. Aisle was founded in 2024 and has built AI systems that detect and help address vulnerabilities in software. Aisle said it had found more than 500 previously unknown vulnerabilities in more than 100 code bases in the past year, and said its platform has matched or outperformed competing systems. “Aisle has been focused on defending the critical infrastructure of the open source ecosystem, and it’s done that better than many of the more well known efforts,” Cohere chief executive officer Aidan Gomez wrote on LinkedIn. Scientists push for creation of international body to regulate artificial intelligence In a blog post, Cohere said that it will combine Aisle’s autonomous security research with its AI models. “The capabilities of a foundation model and the specialized system built around it can reinforce each other,” the company said. Cohere also said it will make a substantial investment in Prague to expand Aisle’s existing presence and establish the city as its global hub for AI cybersecurity systems. Aisle is not Cohere’s first acquisition. In May, it announced the purchase of biopharma company Reliant AI, which has operations in Montreal and Berlin. Cohere also announced a deal to combine with German AI company Aleph Alpha this year, which still requires regulatory approval. The Globe and Mail previously reported that Cohere is in talks to raise upward of US$3-billion, including funds from the Canadian and German governments that would value the company at US$20-billion. The cybersecurity risks of AI have been heightened ever since Anthropic announced its Mythos model earlier this year, which the company said was adept at finding software vulnerabilities. Anthropic initially limited access to a select group of companies to shore up their defences, and has since made it available to qualifying security professionals. More recently, businesses, governments and regulators have become deeply concerned about instances of AI agents breaking free of testing sandboxes to access the internet. Agents from OpenAI, for example, have infiltrated the systems of the Australian government and AI company Hugging Face, while an Anthropic agent submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia police. “You might think, ‘Oh, this is a renaissance for cyber attackers. They have these models that just exploit systems,’ ” Cohere co-founder Ivan Zhang said in an interview. But companies engaged in cyberdefence have an advantage, he continued. “It’s actually easier to patch vulnerabilities than it is to discover them and chain them together to attack a target.” U.S. FTC subpoenas OpenAI, Anthropic over safety incidents, report says Aisle co-founder Ondrej Vlcek will become senior vice-president of Cohere Cyber, a newly established division. Fellow co-founder Jaya Baloo will assume the role of Cohere’s chief information security officer, while Stanislav Fort will become vice-president of AI security. The three co-founders have previously worked at Google DeepMind, Anthropic and Czech cybersecurity company Avast. Mr. Vlcek wrote on LinkedIn that Cohere and Aisle began talking earlier this year and realized that combining would be a “natural fit.” The companies are also pitching the deal as a sign of the deepening ties between Canada and Europe, when relations with the United States are frayed and the AI industry is dominated by American tech giants. “I’ve been hearing how Europe is behind in AI, and how Canada is behind in AI,” Mr. Vlcek wrote. “We can either keep complaining about it, or do something about it.” Report an editorial error Report a technical issue Editorial code of conduct Related stories Cohere signs letter of intent to buy AI cybersecurity startup Aisle Cohere catches Alibaba AI model trying to upload file to Beijing server Ottawa buys $1.6-billion stake in Cohere as AI firm’s valuation soars to $35.7-billion Cohere signs letter of intent to buy AI cybersecurity startup Aisle Cohere catches Alibaba AI model trying to upload file to Beijing server Ottawa buys $1.6-billion stake in Cohere as AI firm’s valuation soars to $35.7-billion Investing opinion & analysis The BoC’s rate hike is totally unnecessary and premature David Rosenberg Insider Report: BlackBerry’s CEO cashes out $2-million Jennifer Dowty Is space the next frontier for investors?
